themes.label: Ownership
themes.description: Taking end-to-end responsibility for outcomes, including problems outside your formal remit.

themes.label: Technical Leadership
themes.description: Setting technical direction, making sound architectural calls, and raising the engineering bar.

themes.label: Influence Without Authority
themes.description: Driving alignment and change across people and teams you do not manage.

themes.label: Conflict
themes.description: Handling disagreements, technical or interpersonal, constructively and reaching a decision.

themes.label: Failure & Learning
themes.description: Owning mistakes, running blameless retrospectives, and turning failures into lasting improvements.

themes.label: Ambiguity
themes.description: Making progress and good decisions when requirements, data, or ownership are unclear.

themes.label: Mentoring
themes.description: Growing other engineers through coaching, feedback, and delegation of meaningful work.

themes.label: Customer Impact
themes.description: Connecting technical work to measurable outcomes for users and the business.

themes.label: Delivery Under Pressure
themes.description: Shipping reliably under constraints by making explicit, well-reasoned trade-offs.

themes.label: Cross-Team Collaboration
themes.description: Working effectively across team, org, and functional boundaries toward shared goals.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you took ownership of a project that was at risk of failing and drove it to completion.
questions.assesses: Whether you step in proactively, diagnose root causes of slippage, and own the outcome rather than just your tasks.
strongSignals: Identified risk early using concrete signals (burndown, missed milestones, dependency slips)
Re-scoped or re-planned explicitly with stakeholders rather than heroics alone
Unblocked others, not just themselves
Quantified outcome (shipped date vs. plan, scope delivered, adoption)
redFlags: Blames others for the risk without describing own actions
followUps: What would you have done if you had noticed the risk a month earlier?
What did you cut, and how did you decide?
How did you communicate the change to stakeholders?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you defined the technical direction for a system when the requirements were still unclear.
questions.assesses: Ability to turn a fuzzy problem into a concrete, reversible technical plan that others can execute on.
strongSignals: Separated known constraints from assumptions and validated the riskiest assumptions first
Wrote a design doc or RFC with alternatives and explicit trade-offs
Chose designs that kept options open (two-way doors) where uncertainty was high
Set checkpoints to revisit decisions as data arrived
redFlags: Waited for complete requirements before acting
Picked a technology because it was familiar or trendy with no trade-off analysis
Plan was never revisited after new information
followUps: Which assumption turned out to be wrong, and how did you adapt?
How did you get buy-in on the direction?
What would you design differently today?

questions.text: Describe a time you convinced another team to adopt a technical approach they were initially skeptical of.
questions.assesses: Whether you can persuade peers with data and empathy rather than authority or persistence.
strongSignals: Understood the other team's incentives and objections before pitching
Used data, prototypes, or benchmarks to make the case
Adjusted the proposal based on their feedback
Reduced adoption cost (migration tooling, docs, pairing)
redFlags: Escalated to management as the first tactic
Treats skepticism as the other team being wrong
followUps: What was their strongest objection, and was it valid?
What would you have done if they had said no?
How did you measure whether adoption succeeded?

questions.text: Tell me about a significant technical disagreement you had with a peer or senior engineer. How was it resolved?
questions.assesses: Whether you disagree productively, focus on the problem rather than the person, and can commit once a decision is made.
strongSignals: Clearly articulated both positions fairly, including the merits of the other side
Proposed objective criteria (latency budget, consistency needs, cost) to decide
Reached a decision and committed, even if it was not their preferred option
Relationship stayed intact or improved
redFlags: The other person is portrayed as simply incompetent
Never actually resolved; just moved on
followUps: In hindsight, who was right?
How did you keep the disagreement from becoming personal?
When is it appropriate to disagree and commit?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you made a mistake that had real consequences. What happened and what did you learn?
questions.assesses: Self-awareness, accountability, and whether learning translated into changed behaviour or systems.
strongSignals: Clearly owns their part without deflecting
Describes immediate mitigation and communication
Identifies a root cause beyond 'I was careless'
Implemented a systemic fix (test, guardrail, process) and can show it worked
redFlags: Lesson learned is vague with no behaviour change
followUps: How did you tell your manager or stakeholders?
Has a similar issue happened since?
What guardrail would have caught it?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to decide what to build when customer needs were unclear or conflicting.
questions.assesses: Whether you go to the source to understand customer problems and make defensible prioritization calls.
strongSignals: Talked to customers, support, or field teams directly, or analysed usage data
Reframed requests into underlying problems
Made an explicit prioritization call with rationale
Measured whether the result addressed the need
redFlags: Built whatever the loudest stakeholder asked for
No contact with customer signal at all
followUps: Which customers did you say no to, and how?
What data would have changed your decision?
How did you validate it after launch?

questions.text: Tell me about an engineer you mentored. How did you help them grow, and what was the outcome?
questions.assesses: Whether you invest deliberately in others' growth and can tailor your approach to the individual.
strongSignals: Identified specific growth areas with the mentee rather than generic advice
Delegated stretch work with appropriate support rather than taking over
Gave timely, specific feedback
Concrete outcome (promotion, ownership of a component, leading a design)
redFlags: Took credit for the mentee's work
No observable change in the mentee
followUps: What did you do when they struggled?
How did your approach differ from mentoring someone else?
What did you learn from mentoring them?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you noticed a problem affecting customers that no one was responsible for, and you fixed it.
questions.assesses: Bias for ownership beyond formal boundaries and sensitivity to customer pain.
strongSignals: Noticed the issue via data, support tickets, or own investigation
Quantified the customer impact to justify the work
Coordinated with owning or adjacent teams rather than working around them
Established lasting ownership or monitoring so it would not recur
redFlags: Fixed it silently with no follow-up or owner established
Overstepped by changing other teams' systems without communication
followUps: Why had no one fixed it before?
What did you deprioritise to do this?
Who owns it now?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to deliver under a hard deadline and had to make significant trade-offs.
questions.assesses: Whether trade-offs are explicit, reasoned, and communicated, and whether quality debt is managed rather than hidden.
strongSignals: Distinguished must-haves from nice-to-haves with stakeholders
Protected correctness and reliability while cutting scope
Recorded and later paid down deferred work
Delivered on time with a clear measure of what shipped
redFlags: Cut testing or monitoring without acknowledging the risk
followUps: What did you refuse to compromise on?
What happened to the deferred work?
Would you make the same trade-offs again?

questions.text: Describe a project that required several teams to coordinate. What was your role in making it work?
questions.assesses: Ability to drive cross-team execution: shared plans, interfaces, and communication without formal authority.
strongSignals: Established shared goals, interfaces, and owners early
Created lightweight coordination mechanisms (sync, tracker, API contracts)
Surfaced cross-team risks and resolved them proactively
Outcome measured across the whole effort, not just their slice
redFlags: Only describes their own team's work
Relied on escalation to get other teams to act
followUps: Which team was hardest to align, and why?
How did you handle a dependency that slipped?
What would you change about the coordination model?

questions.text: Walk me through a production incident you were involved in. What was your role during and after it?
questions.assesses: Calm incident handling, mitigation-first thinking, and driving a blameless postmortem to systemic fixes.
strongSignals: Prioritised mitigation (rollback, failover, traffic shift) before root cause
Communicated status clearly to stakeholders during the incident
Led or contributed to a blameless postmortem with root and contributing causes
Drove action items to completion and can cite reduced recurrence or faster detection (MTTD/MTTR)
redFlags: Spent the incident debugging while customers stayed impacted
Postmortem assigned blame to an individual
followUps: How was the incident detected, and could it have been sooner?
What was the most important action item?
How did you make sure it would not recur?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you raised the engineering bar on your team.
questions.assesses: Whether you improve how the team works (quality, practices, standards), not just what you personally produce.
strongSignals: Identified a concrete quality gap backed by evidence (defect rates, incidents, review churn)
Introduced a practice or tooling (design reviews, testing strategy, SLOs) with team buy-in
Made the standard easy to follow, not just mandated
Measured improvement over time
redFlags: Bar-raising amounts to being a strict code reviewer
followUps: Who pushed back, and how did you respond?
Did the change stick after you stopped driving it?
How do you balance standards with velocity?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you needed something from a team that had different priorities. How did you get it done?
questions.assesses: Ability to align incentives across teams and find win-win outcomes rather than forcing priority.
strongSignals: Understood the other team's goals and constraints
Framed the request in terms of shared or business value
Offered to contribute engineering effort or reduce their cost
Reached an agreement with a clear timeline
redFlags: Worked around the team in a way that created hidden coupling
Treated the other team as an obstacle
followUps: What did you offer in return?
What if they had refused entirely?
How is your relationship with that team now?

questions.text: Describe a time you had a conflict with another team over ownership or responsibility for a system.
questions.assesses: Whether you can resolve organisational friction constructively and produce clear ownership.
strongSignals: Focused on the system's health and users rather than turf
Proposed clear boundaries (APIs, runbooks, on-call responsibilities)
Involved the right decision-makers when peers could not agree
Outcome: documented ownership and reduced friction
followUps: What was the root cause of the ambiguity?
When did you decide to involve management?
How did you prevent it recurring for other systems?

questions.text: Tell me about a project that did not meet its goals. What went wrong and what did you do about it?
questions.assesses: Honest reflection on project-level failure and the ability to extract and apply lessons.
strongSignals: Candid about own contribution to the shortfall
Distinguishes between bad decisions and bad outcomes
Took corrective action or salvaged partial value
Applied lessons to later projects with evidence
followUps: When did you first know it was going wrong?
What would you have done differently on day one?
How did you apply this on your next project?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you were given a vague goal and had to figure out what success looked like.
questions.assesses: Ability to define measurable success criteria and break ambiguous goals into deliverable milestones.
strongSignals: Defined concrete, measurable success criteria and got them agreed
Broke work into incremental milestones delivering value early
Clarified with stakeholders iteratively rather than guessing
Delivered against the criteria they defined
redFlags: Waited for someone else to clarify
Success never defined, so outcome is unclear
Built a large solution before validating direction
followUps: Who did you consult to define success?
How did you handle changes to the goal midway?
Did the metrics you chose turn out to be the right ones?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you helped a less experienced engineer lead a technically difficult piece of work.
questions.assesses: Whether you scale yourself by growing technical leaders instead of being the bottleneck.
strongSignals: Deliberately gave ownership rather than retaining it
Coached through design reviews by asking questions rather than dictating
Provided a safety net (review checkpoints, rollback plans) without micromanaging
The engineer grew in visible ways and the work succeeded
redFlags: Took over when it got hard
followUps: When did you choose not to intervene?
What mistake did you let them make?
How did you give them visibility for the work?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to balance shipping a customer-requested feature quickly against long-term system health.
questions.assesses: Judgement in weighing near-term customer value against reliability, maintainability, and operational cost.
strongSignals: Quantified both sides (customer value, revenue, or churn risk versus operational risk)
Found an option that delivered value while limiting long-term cost (feature flag, phased rollout)
Made the trade-off transparent to product and stakeholders
Followed up on both the customer outcome and the system health
redFlags: Ignores reliability or ignores the customer
followUps: How did you quantify the long-term cost?
Who made the final call?
What happened six months later?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you improved something that spanned beyond your team's boundaries, such as shared infrastructure or a platform.
questions.assesses: Scope beyond your own team and the ability to deliver improvements that benefit the wider org.
strongSignals: Identified a problem affecting multiple teams with data
Built a coalition and worked within the owning team's processes
Designed for broad adoption (backward compatibility, migration paths)
Quantified org-wide impact (build time, incidents, cost)
redFlags: Built a parallel solution that fragmented the ecosystem
Impact limited to their own team
followUps: How did you get time allocated for this?
How did you drive adoption?
Who maintains it now?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to give difficult feedback to a colleague.
questions.assesses: Willingness to have hard conversations with care, specificity, and follow-through.
strongSignals: Feedback was specific, behavioural, and timely
Delivered privately and with empathy, focused on impact
Listened to the other person's perspective
Followed up and saw change
redFlags: Avoided it or went straight to the manager
followUps: How did they react?
What would you do if nothing changed?
How do you ask for feedback yourself?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to make an important technical decision with incomplete data.
questions.assesses: Decision quality under uncertainty: gathering just enough information, judging reversibility, and managing risk.
strongSignals: Distinguished reversible from irreversible decisions and calibrated speed accordingly
Gathered the highest-value data quickly (spike, benchmark, load test)
Made the decision with explicit assumptions and mitigations
Defined signals that would trigger revisiting the decision
redFlags: Decided on gut with no risk mitigation
followUps: What information did you wish you had?
How did you communicate the uncertainty?
How did the decision turn out?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you changed your organisation's or product team's priorities based on customer or operational evidence.
questions.assesses: Ability to use evidence to influence roadmap decisions beyond engineering.
strongSignals: Collected compelling evidence (support data, telemetry, incident trends, customer interviews)
Framed it in business terms decision-makers cared about
Proposed a concrete alternative plan
Priority changed and outcome was measured
followUps: Who was hardest to convince?
What got dropped as a result?
Was the reprioritisation the right call in hindsight?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager's or leadership's decision.
questions.assesses: Whether you voice disagreement candidly through appropriate channels and then commit or escalate sensibly.
strongSignals: Raised concerns with data and a constructive alternative
Understood context the manager had that they did not
Disagreed and committed, or changed the decision through evidence
Maintained trust
redFlags: Undermined the decision after it was made
followUps: What context were you missing?
What would have made you escalate further?
How did it turn out?

questions.text: Tell me about a time someone you were mentoring or leading made a mistake that reached production. How did you handle it?
questions.assesses: Whether you build psychological safety and treat failures as system issues and learning opportunities.
strongSignals: Shielded the individual from blame while ensuring accountability
Helped them lead or participate in the postmortem
Fixed the systemic gap (review, testing, deployment guardrails)
The engineer's confidence and skills grew afterward
redFlags: Fixed it themselves without involving the engineer
followUps: What process gap allowed it?
How did you talk with the engineer afterwards?
What did the team learn?

questions.text: Tell me about a time a dependency on another team put your project at risk.
questions.assesses: Proactive dependency management and constructive collaboration under schedule pressure.
strongSignals: Identified the dependency risk early and agreed on contracts or timelines
Communicated impact clearly and without blame
Explored options (contributing code, interim workaround, re-sequencing)
Delivered with minimal impact and improved future coordination
redFlags: Built a fragile workaround with no plan to remove it
followUps: What early warning signs did you miss?
How did you decide between waiting and working around it?
What did you change for future projects?

questions.text: Tell me about a system you designed or significantly changed to improve its reliability.
questions.assesses: Designing for reliability: understanding failure modes, observability, and measurable resilience improvements.
strongSignals: Started from data (incident history, SLO burn, error budgets)
Addressed specific failure modes (retries with backoff, idempotency, replication, graceful degradation)
Added observability and alerting tied to user impact
Quantified improvement (availability, p99 latency, incident count, MTTR)
redFlags: Reliability work is vague or purely reactive
followUps: Which failure mode worried you most?
How did you test the failure handling?
How did you justify the investment?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to decide whether to pay down technical debt or build new features.
questions.assesses: Ability to articulate the cost of technical debt in business terms and make balanced investment decisions.
strongSignals: Quantified the debt's cost (velocity drag, incidents, on-call load)
Proposed incremental paydown alongside feature work
Got stakeholder agreement on the trade-off
Measured the result after paydown
redFlags: Cannot express debt in terms of impact
followUps: How did you convince product to invest?
How did you choose which debt to tackle first?
What debt did you consciously leave?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you changed how your team works, such as code review, on-call, or design review, without being the manager.
questions.assesses: Ability to improve team culture and practices through influence and by modelling the behaviour.
strongSignals: Identified the problem with evidence and team input
Piloted the change and iterated on feedback
Modelled the behaviour and coached others into it
Change persisted and produced measurable improvement
followUps: Who resisted, and why?
How did you know it was working?
What did you change after the pilot?

questions.text: Tell me about a time a decision or release of yours negatively affected customers.
questions.assesses: Customer-centred accountability: owning impact, communicating transparently, and preventing recurrence.
strongSignals: Quantified customer impact honestly
Prioritised mitigation and customer communication
Worked with support or customer-facing teams on remediation
Changed release practices (canaries, flags, staged rollout) to prevent recurrence
redFlags: Treats it as purely a technical bug with no process lesson
followUps: How did customers find out?
What would a staged rollout have changed?
How did you rebuild trust?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked with non-engineering partners, such as product, support, or sales, on a poorly defined problem.
questions.assesses: Ability to bridge functions, translate between technical and business language, and converge on a shared definition of the problem.
strongSignals: Translated technical constraints into terms partners understood
Facilitated agreement on the problem before solutions
Kept partners informed with regular, appropriate updates
Outcome valued by both engineering and the partner function
followUps: Where did your understanding of the problem differ from theirs?
How did you handle a request that was technically infeasible?
What did you learn about their function?

starGuide.situation: Set context in one or two sentences: the team, the system, the scale, and why the stakes mattered. Skip background the interviewer does not need.
starGuide.task: State your specific responsibility and the goal, making clear what was yours versus the team's, and what made it hard (ambiguity, deadline, cross-team scope).
starGuide.action: Spend most of your answer here, using 'I' not 'we': the options you considered, the trade-offs, how you influenced others, and why you chose what you did.
starGuide.result: Quantify the outcome (latency, availability, incidents, adoption, time saved, revenue), then name what you learned or would do differently and how it changed your later work.
